messages.subject: nested indexing
parts:
Does STAN support nested indexing as a way to deal with missing/unbalanced data? In case my question is not clear, here's an example from the open bugs guide http://www.openbugs.info/Manuals/Tricks.html :

"Suppose we observe the following data on three individuals:

      Person 1: 13.2
      Person 2: 12.3 , 14.1
      Person 3: 11.0, 9.7, 10.3, 9.6

2. Nested indexing: Here the data are stored in a single array and the associated person is recorded as a factor, i.e.

       y[]   person[]
       13.2   1
       12.3   2
       14.1   2
       11.0   3
       9.7   3
       10.3   3
       9.6   3
      END

or list(y = c(13.2, 12.3, 14.1, 11.0, 9.7, 10.3, 9.6), person = c(1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 3)).

A model such as y[k] ~ dnorm(mu[person[k]], 1) can then be fitted."

Best,
  Ian

   real y[Ndata]; 
}

I think someone already replied, but just in case not,
the problem is that you need to assign mu[r] BEFORE
you use it in the sampling statement.

Unlike BUGS, there's no reason to make mu an array.
You can reassign local variables in Stan.

You can also just drop the expression for mu into the
first argument position (location) for the normal. It's
roughly equally efficient either way.

You have the same problem with sigma -- using it before
it is defined. But this one's a deeper problem.
sigma should be a parameter here as it's on the left side
of a sampling twiddle (~). Just declaring it as a local
leaves it undefined when you hit

sigma[s] ~ gamma(.01,.01);

which just translates into C++ as:

lp__ += gamma_log(sigma[s], .01, .01);

It is legal to have things other than params on the LHS
of twiddle, but not if they're supposed to be variable.
You can put transformed params there, but then it's up
to you to add the log Jacobian into the lp__ term.

Having said all that, the order of sampling statements
doesn't matter. Parameters and transformed parameters
are all defined before you enter the model block execution.

- Bob

I think someone already replied, but just in case not,
the problem is that you need to assign mu[r] BEFORE
you use it in the sampling statement.

Unlike BUGS, there's no reason to make mu an array.
You can reassign local variables in Stan.

You can also just drop the expression for mu into the
first argument position (location) for the normal.  It's
roughly equally efficient either way.

You have the same problem with sigma -- using it before
it is defined.  But this one's a deeper problem.
sigma should be a parameter here as it's on the left side
of a sampling twiddle (~).  Just declaring it as a local
leaves it undefined when you hit

          sigma[s] ~ gamma(.01,.01);

which just translates into C++ as:

    lp__ += gamma_log(sigma[s], .01, .01);

It is legal to have things other than params on the LHS
of twiddle, but not if they're supposed to be variable.
You can put transformed params there, but then it's up
to you to add the log Jacobian into the lp__ term.

Having said all that, the order of sampling statements
doesn't matter.  Parameters and transformed parameters
are all defined before you enter the model block execution.

- Bob

On Tuesday, September 4, 2012 2:22:36 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
I think someone already replied, but just in case not,
the problem is that you need to assign mu[r] BEFORE
you use it in the sampling statement.

Unlike BUGS, there's no reason to make mu an array.
You can reassign local variables in Stan.

You can also just drop the expression for mu into the
first argument position (location) for the normal.  It's
roughly equally efficient either way.

You have the same problem with sigma -- using it before
it is defined.  But this one's a deeper problem.
sigma should be a parameter here as it's on the left side
of a sampling twiddle (~).  Just declaring it as a local
leaves it undefined when you hit

          sigma[s] ~ gamma(.01,.01);

which just translates into C++ as:

    lp__ += gamma_log(sigma[s], .01, .01);

It is legal to have things other than params on the LHS
of twiddle, but not if they're supposed to be variable.
You can put transformed params there, but then it's up
to you to add the log Jacobian into the lp__ term.

Having said all that, the order of sampling statements
doesn't matter.  Parameters and transformed parameters
are all defined before you enter the model block execution.

- Bob
